title: The wind as incense
hook: tradition sets this hymn at Puri, where Nanak saw a temple aarti and pointed to the one the universe performs

segments.voice: Yesterday, aarti; your line was you don't light it, you notice it. Today, the story Sikhs tell about where this hymn was first sung.
screen: `AARTI — YOU DON'T LIGHT IT, YOU NOTICE IT.`

segments.voice: The east coast of India, on the Bay of Bengal. A town called Puri, home to the great temple of Jagannath, Lord of the World. Pilgrims still walk there. The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life, say he came here on his long journeys with his companion Mardana, the musician who played the rabab. Evening came, and the temple's aarti began: lamps on golden trays, incense, bells, crowds. And the stories say Guru Nanak stood quietly and didn't join in.
screen: `PURI, ON THE BAY OF BENGAL.` → `NANAK AND MARDANA ARRIVE.` → `THE EVENING AARTI BEGINS.`

segments.voice: In one telling, someone notices the visitor standing apart and asks why. In reply, Guru Nanak asks Mardana to play, and he sings: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. The fragrant breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, the forests are the flowers. What a wonderful aarti this is. The aarti, he says, has been going on the whole time. It's just bigger than the temple. Hold this story as tradition. The hymn itself doesn't name Puri, and the janamsakhis were written down after Guru Nanak's lifetime and don't always agree in detail. What the hymn does say, in its later verses, turns the picture inside out. In paraphrase: You have thousands of eyes, and yet no eye; thousands of forms, and yet not one form; thousands of feet, yet no foot; thousands of noses, yet no nose. And then: within everything is a light, and that light is You. By that light, all are lit. So the wind isn't only incense. The wind, the stars, the forests, the people at the temple, the people standing apart: all lit by the same light. The story, as Sikhs tell it, isn't about scorning anybody's lamps. It widens the circle until the whole world is inside the offering, the priests, the pilgrims and the two travelers too.
screen: `WHY AREN'T YOU JOINING IN?` · `THE AARTI HAS BEEN GOING ON ALL ALONG.` · `THOUSANDS OF EYES, YET NO EYE.` · `ONE LIGHT, AND ALL ARE LIT.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Open a window, step outside, or just breathe in slowly where you are: cut grass, rain, someone's cooking, the dry air of a vent. Whatever it is, let it be the incense in the hymn, carried to you on the wind. Breathe out slowly, and if you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.
Pavan, wind or breeze: in Sohila's third hymn, the breeze carries the fragrance and the wind waves the fan, the whole world performing the aarti.
Your line: the whole world offering. In the hymn's picture, the aarti never stops. That's day four hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly in Kirtan Sohila and sing it in gurdwaras as the Aarti; the story of Guru Nanak at Puri is often told alongside it, especially at gurdwara evening programs.

notes: Puri story told as tradition (janamsakhi); details vary between janamsakhis. Confirm the version (Nanak asked why he did not join, Mardana plays, he sings the hymn) is the common one.
Later verses paraphrased ('thousands of eyes, and yet no eye; thousands of forms, and yet not one form'; 'within everything is a light, and that light is You; by that light all are lit'). Confirm.
Tone toward the temple aarti: written to avoid scorn and to present the story as widening the circle; confirm a Keeper is comfortable.
Gurmukhi ਪਵਨ (the hymn has the form pavan/pavanu); confirm.
